topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
summary:
This topic covers interactive data collection and structured tabular presentation in HTML5. Forms provide the primary interface between users and backend servers, governed by the `
` container with critical attributes `action` (processing endpoint), `method` (`GET` which appends data to the URL query string vs `POST` which transmits data securely in the request body), and `enctype` (`multipart/form-data` required for binary file uploads). Form controls include `` (text, password, email, number, date, radio, checkbox, file, submit), `

key_terms.definition: The HTTP form transmission method that packages form data inside the HTTP request body; it does not expose data in the browser URL, is not cached, has no strict length limits, and is mandatory for sensitive data and file uploads.

The default HTTP form submission method that appends form key-value pairs directly to the action URL as a query string; data is visible in the browser address bar, cached in history, and subject to ~2048 character length limits.
The required form encoding attribute when submitting binary files via <input type='file'>; without it, the browser sends only the string filename rather than the actual file contents.
An HTML table cell attribute (used on <th> or <td>) that specifies the number of horizontal columns the cell should span across.
An HTML table cell attribute (used on <th> or <td>) that specifies the number of vertical rows the cell should span down.
A set of <input type='radio'> controls that share the exact same 'name' attribute, enforcing mutual exclusivity where selecting one option automatically deselects all other options in that group.
Attributes restricting input editing: 'disabled' grays out the field and EXCLUDES it from form submission; 'readonly' prevents user edits but INCLUDES the value in the form submission.
A mandatory attribute on elements providing alternative text for screen readers (accessibility) and displaying fallback text if the image asset fails to load.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: A student builds a university login form with `<form action="login.php" method="GET">`. What security vulnerability and behavioral defect immediately occurs when a user submits their password?
options: The server will refuse to turn on its cooling fans

The student's password is appended directly to the browser URL address bar in clear readable text (e.g., `login.php?user=aliyu&pass=secret123`), storing it in browser history, proxy server logs, and displaying it on screen
The browser will automatically delete the student's operating system
The form will only submit if the student writes the password backwards
questions.explanation: Form submissions using `method="GET"` append all form inputs directly onto the URL as query parameters. This exposes passwords in browser address bars, browser history, server access logs, and HTTP referer headers. Login forms, passwords, and sensitive financial transactions MUST always use `method="POST"`.

why_wrong.0: HTTP methods are software protocol mechanisms; they do not control physical server cooling hardware.
why_wrong.2: Submitting a GET form does not delete operating system files.
why_wrong.3: Browsers submit string values exactly as typed; they do not reverse text.

questions.source: IFT 203 Week 5 Slides; Practice Codes Docx; MDN Form Methods

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: When creating an HTML form that includes a passport photograph upload (`<input type="file" name="photo">`), which attribute MUST be explicitly included in the `<form>` opening tag?
options: `enctype="text/plain"`
`enctype="multipart/form-data"` along with `method="POST"`
`method="GET"` and `target="_blank"`
`enctype="application/json"` with `autocomplete="off"`
questions.explanation: Standard forms use `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. To transmit binary files (images, PDFs) to the server, the form MUST specify `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and use `method="POST"`. If omitted, the browser only sends the string name of the file instead of the binary byte data.

why_wrong.0: `text/plain` sends unencoded text without boundary delimiters, corrupting binary image data.
why_wrong.2: `GET` cannot upload binary files because data is restricted to URL strings.
why_wrong.3: `application/json` is not a standard native HTML form enctype attribute for binary file streaming.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question:
Analyze the following table code: ```html
Time Monday Tuesday
9:00 AM COS 201 Practical Lab
11:00 AM IFT 203 SEN 201
``` How will the cell containing `COS 201 Practical Lab` be rendered visually?
options: It will be rendered only under Monday, leaving Tuesday's column completely empty
It will span horizontally across BOTH the Monday and Tuesday columns in the 9:00 AM row
It will span vertically down into the 11:00 AM row
It will cause an error and prevent the table from displaying
questions.explanation: The attribute `colspan="2"` instructs the table rendering engine to merge that single `<td>` cell horizontally across two column widths. Because the header row defines 3 total columns (Time, Monday, Tuesday), the second row consists of 1 cell for Time plus 1 cell spanning 2 columns, creating a perfectly balanced 3-column table row.

why_wrong.0: A `colspan="2"` cell explicitly expands across two columns, covering both Monday and Tuesday.
why_wrong.2: Vertical spanning across rows is achieved using `rowspan`, not `colspan`.
why_wrong.3: `colspan` is a standard HTML table attribute and does not throw errors.

questions.question: Order the structural child elements of a fully compliant semantic HTML5 table from top to bottom as they should be nested inside `<table>`:
options: <caption> (accessible title of the table, placed first)
<thead> containing <tr> and <th> header cells
<tbody> containing <tr> and <td> data rows
<tfoot> containing <tr> and <td> summary or total calculations
answer: <caption> (accessible title of the table, placed first)
<tfoot> containing <tr> and <td> summary or total calculations
questions.explanation: In semantic HTML tables: `<caption>` must appear immediately after `<table>`, followed by `<thead>` (headers), `<tbody>` (data rows), and `<tfoot>` (footer totals/summaries).

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question:
A form contains two non-editable fields:
`Field A: <input type="text" name="matric" value="2024/001" readonly>`
`Field B: <input type="text" name="role" value="Student" disabled>`
When the user clicks the submit button, what data is sent to the backend server?
options: Neither Field A nor Field B will be submitted
`matric=2024/001` will be submitted, but `role` will NOT be submitted at all
`role=Student` will be submitted, but `matric` will NOT be submitted
Both `matric` and `role` will be submitted normally
questions.explanation: This is a classic web examiner trap. The `readonly` attribute prevents the user from altering the text, but the field's `name` and `value` ARE included in form submission. In contrast, the `disabled` attribute grays out the field AND completely excludes the field from form submission (it is not sent in the HTTP payload).

why_wrong.0: `readonly` fields are always submitted with the form data.
why_wrong.2: `disabled` fields are omitted from form payloads; `role` is not sent.
why_wrong.3: `disabled` prevents Field B from being transmitted to the server.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: What is the difference between `method="GET"` and `method="POST"` in an HTML form?
questions.answer:
GET appends data to the URL query string (visible, cached, ~2KB limit, for searches/lookups).
POST sends data in the HTTP request body (invisible in URL, uncached, no size limits, mandatory for logins, passwords, and file uploads).
questions.explanation: Crucial distinction tested in all web development exams.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: What form attribute is required when uploading files, and what happens if it is omitted?
questions.answer: The form MUST specify `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and `method="POST"`. If omitted, the browser defaults to `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and sends only the filename string, not the actual file contents.
questions.explanation: Covered in IFT 203 Week 5 and the Student Registration code practical.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: How do you make a group of `<input type="radio">` buttons mutually exclusive?
questions.answer: By giving all radio buttons in that group the EXACT same `name` attribute (e.g., `name="level"`). The browser then permits only one option to be checked at a time.
questions.explanation: To create a mutually exclusive radio button group, all '<input type="radio">' elements in the group must share the exact same 'name' attribute value. The browser will then permit only one radio button in that group to be checked at any given time. (W3C HTML5 Specification).

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: What is the purpose of the `<label for="xyz">` element?
questions.answer: It binds a text label to an input with `id="xyz"`. It enhances accessibility for screen readers and allows users to click the text label to focus or toggle the input control.
questions.explanation: The '<label for="element-id">' element provides a programmatic association between a descriptive text label and a form control. Clicking the label focuses or toggles the input (vital for small mobile touch targets on checkboxes/radios), and screen readers announce the label text when the input receives focus. (W3C Web Content Accessibility Guidelines - WCAG 2.1).

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: Explain the difference between `colspan` and `rowspan` in an HTML table.
questions.answer:
`colspan="n"` merges a cell horizontally across $n$ columns.
`rowspan="n"` merges a cell vertically down across $n$ rows.
questions.explanation: Essential for creating complex academic timetables and report grids.

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: What is the key difference between `readonly` and `disabled` on form inputs during submission?
questions.answer: A `readonly` field cannot be modified by the user, but its value IS submitted to the server. A `disabled` field is grayed out and its value is NOT submitted to the server.
questions.explanation: The fundamental difference between form control states: A 'readonly' input prevents user editing but its value IS submitted with the form payload during submission. A 'disabled' input is greyed out, cannot be focused or modified, and its value is strictly EXCLUDED from the submitted form data payload. (W3C HTML5 Form Submission).

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: Why is the `alt` attribute mandatory on all `` tags?
questions.answer:
1. Accessibility: Screen readers read the alt text aloud to visually impaired users.
2. Fallback: Displays description if the image file fails to load.
3. SEO: Enables search engine web crawlers to index image content.
questions.explanation: The 'alt' (alternative text) attribute on '' elements is mandatory under WCAG guidelines: screen readers read it aloud to visually impaired users, web crawlers use it for search engine indexing, and browsers display it as a fallback if the image asset fails to load. Empty 'alt=""' is reserved only for purely decorative images. (WCAG 2.1 Principle 1: Perceivable).

questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
questions.question: Why should `<a href="..." target="_blank">` always be paired with `rel="noopener noreferrer"`?
questions.answer: For security: without it, the newly opened external page can access your page's JavaScript execution context via `window.opener` and redirect your users to a malicious phishing site (known as reverse tabnabbing).
questions.explanation: When opening links in a new tab via 'target="_blank"', modern web security requires adding 'rel="noopener noreferrer"'. Without 'noopener', the target page gains access to the originating window's 'window.opener' object, enabling malicious reverse tabnabbing phishing attacks. (MDN Web Security; OWASP Foundation).
questions.source: MDN Web Security; IFT 203 Lecture Notes

sub_questions.question: Which set of modifications completely resolves ALL THREE defects in this student registration form?

case_studies.scenario: A departmental administrator is creating the official 200-Level First Semester Timetable grid in HTML for the Department of Information Technology. The timetable spans 4 periods (9-10 AM, 10-11 AM, 11-12 PM, 12-1 PM) across Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday. The schedule has three special constraints: (1) On Monday, 'COS 201 Practical Lab' occupies a double period (9-11 AM); (2) Every day at 11-12 PM, all students attend a university-wide 'Assembly / Break'; (3) The table must be accessible with caption and semantic headers.

sub_questions.topic: HTML Forms, Inputs, Tables & Media Elements
sub_questions.question: If 'Assembly / Break' occurs at 11-12 PM across ALL THREE DAYS (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday), and the developer wants to represent it with a single merged table cell in a table where Days are columns and Time periods are rows, which attribute must be used?
options: `rowspan="3"`
`colspan="3"`
`cellpadding="3"`
`border="3"`
sub_questions.explanation: Because Days (Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday) are columns, merging across all three days within the 11-12 PM row is horizontal spanning across columns, which requires `colspan="3"`.

why_wrong.0: `rowspan="3"` would merge vertically down across three different time periods on a single day.
why_wrong.2: `cellpadding` controls internal pixel padding, not column merging.
why_wrong.3: `border="3"` sets border line thickness, not cell span.
